claim: Lam/GramD1 proteins are a family of endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins with sterol-binding StARkin domains.
source: Previously we identified Lam/GramD1 proteins, a family of endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins with sterol-binding StARkin domains that are implicated in intracellular sterol homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Lam/GramD1 proteins are implicated in intracellular sterol homeostasis.
source: Previously we identified Lam/GramD1 proteins, a family of endoplasmic reticulum membrane proteins with sterol-binding StARkin domains that are implicated in intracellular sterol homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by prior research.

claim: An aperture at one end of the StARkin domain enables sterol to enter/exit the binding pocket.
source: An aperture at one end of the StARkin domain enables sterol to enter/exit the binding pocket.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural analysis and MD simulations.

claim: The wall of the sterol-binding pocket is longitudinally fractured, exposing bound sterol to solvent.
source: Strikingly, the wall of the pocket is longitudinally fractured, exposing bound sterol to solvent.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: Sterol egress involves widening of the fracture in the binding pocket wall.
source: Large-scale atomistic molecular dynamics simulations reveal that sterol egress involves widening of the fracture, penetration of water into the cavity, and consequent destabilization of the bound sterol.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Sterol egress involves penetration of water into the binding cavity.
source: Large-scale atomistic molecular dynamics simulations reveal that sterol egress involves widening of the fracture, penetration of water into the cavity, and consequent destabilization of the bound sterol.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by MD simulation data showing water penetration.

claim: Water penetration into the binding cavity leads to destabilization of the bound sterol.
source: Large-scale atomistic molecular dynamics simulations reveal that sterol egress involves widening of the fracture, penetration of water into the cavity, and consequent destabilization of the bound sterol.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Polar residues along the fracture are important for sterol release.
source: The simulations identify polar residues along the fracture that are important for sterol release.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by computational and experimental data.

claim: Replacement of polar residues along the fracture with alanine affects the ability of the StARkin domain to bind sterol.
source: Their replacement with alanine affects the ability of the StARkin domain to bind sterol, catalyze inter-vesicular sterol exchange and alleviate the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ yeast cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Replacement of polar residues along the fracture with alanine affects the ability of the StARkin domain to catalyze inter-vesicular sterol exchange.
source: Their replacement with alanine affects the ability of the StARkin domain to bind sterol, catalyze inter-vesicular sterol exchange and alleviate the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ yeast cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Replacement of polar residues along the fracture with alanine affects the ability of the StARkin domain to alleviate the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ yeast cells.
source: Their replacement with alanine affects the ability of the StARkin domain to bind sterol, catalyze inter-vesicular sterol exchange and alleviate the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ yeast cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: Cholesterol is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Like many membrane lipids, it is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and transported to the PM by non-vesicular mechanisms that make use of lipid transport proteins (Holthuis and Menon, 2014; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Cholesterol is transported to the plasma membrane by non-vesicular mechanisms that use lipid transport proteins.
source: Like many membrane lipids, it is synthesized in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and transported to the PM by non-vesicular mechanisms that make use of lipid transport proteins (Holthuis and Menon, 2014; Wong et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Lipid transport proteins operate as intracellular molecular ferries.
source: These proteins operate as intracellular molecular ferries, achieving lipid exchange between membranes by reversibly extracting a lipid from the cytoplasmic leaflet of one membrane bilayer, encapsulating it within a binding pocket for transfer through the cytoplasm, and depositing it in the cytoplasmic leaflet of another membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Lipid transport proteins achieve lipid exchange by reversibly extracting a lipid from one membrane, encapsulating it, and depositing it in another membrane.
source: These proteins operate as intracellular molecular ferries, achieving lipid exchange between membranes by reversibly extracting a lipid from the cytoplasmic leaflet of one membrane bilayer, encapsulating it within a binding pocket for transfer through the cytoplasm, and depositing it in the cytoplasmic leaflet of another membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Proteins containing StART domains constitute a major family of intracellular lipid transport proteins.
source: Proteins that contain steroidogenic acute regulatory protein related lipid transfer (StART) domains constitute a major family of intracellular lipid transport proteins — the StARkin superfamily.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: StARkin superfamily proteins are generally soluble and able to diffuse freely through the cytoplasm.
source: Proteins of this family are generally soluble and able to diffuse freely through the cytoplasm, and they are implicated in moving glycerophospholipids, ceramide and sterol between cellular membranes (Wong and Levine, 2016; Alpy and Tomasetto, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: StARkin superfamily proteins are implicated in moving glycerophospholipids, ceramide and sterol between cellular membranes.
source: Proteins of this family are generally soluble and able to diffuse freely through the cytoplasm, and they are implicated in moving glycerophospholipids, ceramide and sterol between cellular membranes (Wong and Levine, 2016; Alpy and Tomasetto, 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: A new family of ER membrane proteins with cytoplasmically disposed StARkin domains was recently identified.
source: A new family of ER membrane proteins that have cytoplasmically disposed StARkin domains was recently identified, including six members (Lam1–Lam6) in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and three members (GramD1a–GramD1c, also termed Aster-A–C) in mammals (Gatta et al., 2015; Elbaz-Alon et al., 2015; Murley et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2009; Sandhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The Lam/GramD1 family includes six members (Lam1–Lam6) in budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: A new family of ER membrane proteins that have cytoplasmically disposed StARkin domains was recently identified, including six members (Lam1–Lam6) in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and three members (GramD1a–GramD1c, also termed Aster-A–C) in mammals (Gatta et al., 2015; Elbaz-Alon et al., 2015; Murley et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2009; Sandhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The Lam/GramD1 family includes three members (GramD1a–GramD1c, also termed Aster-A–C) in mammals.
source: A new family of ER membrane proteins that have cytoplasmically disposed StARkin domains was recently identified, including six members (Lam1–Lam6) in the budding yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and three members (GramD1a–GramD1c, also termed Aster-A–C) in mammals (Gatta et al., 2015; Elbaz-Alon et al., 2015; Murley et al., 2015; Sullivan et al., 2009; Sandhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Members of the Lam/GramD1 family have one or two StARkin domains that bind sterols.
source: Members of this new sub-family have one or two StARkin domains that bind sterols and catalyze sterol exchange between populations of vesicles in vitro (Gatta et al., 2015; Murley et al., 2015; Sandhu et al., 2018; Jentsch et al., 2018; Horenkamp et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Members of the Lam/GramD1 family catalyze sterol exchange between populations of vesicles in vitro.
source: Members of this new sub-family have one or two StARkin domains that bind sterols and catalyze sterol exchange between populations of vesicles in vitro (Gatta et al., 2015; Murley et al., 2015; Sandhu et al., 2018; Jentsch et al., 2018; Horenkamp et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Lam1–Lam4 localize to ER–PM contact sites in yeast.
source: Lam1–Lam4 localize to ER–PM contact sites in yeast (Gatta et al., 2015; Quon et al., 2018) where they play a role in sterol homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Lam1–Lam4 play a role in sterol homeostasis in yeast.
source: Lam1–Lam4 localize to ER–PM contact sites in yeast (Gatta et al., 2015; Quon et al., 2018) where they play a role in sterol homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Yeast cells lacking one or more Lam proteins are hypersensitive to sterol-binding polyene antibiotics amphotericin and nystatin.
source: Thus, yeast cells that lack one or more of these proteins are hypersensitive to the sterol-binding polyene antibiotics amphotericin and nystatin, implying that they have alterations in PM sterol content and/or organization (Gatta et al., 2015; Roelants et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Hypersensitivity of Lam-deficient yeast cells to polyene antibiotics implies alterations in PM sterol content and/or organization.
source: Thus, yeast cells that lack one or more of these proteins are hypersensitive to the sterol-binding polyene antibiotics amphotericin and nystatin, implying that they have alterations in PM sterol content and/or organization (Gatta et al., 2015; Roelants et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Lam-deficient yeast cells esterify exogenously supplied sterols up to 3-fold more slowly than wild-type cells.
source: Furthermore, they esterify exogenously supplied sterols up to 3-fold more slowly than wild-type cells, indicating a delay in some aspect of PM–ER sterol transport (Gatta et al., 2015; Roelants et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Slower sterol esterification in Lam-deficient yeast cells indicates a delay in PM–ER sterol transport.
source: Furthermore, they esterify exogenously supplied sterols up to 3-fold more slowly than wild-type cells, indicating a delay in some aspect of PM–ER sterol transport (Gatta et al., 2015; Roelants et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Mouse GramD1b (Aster-B) protein is highly expressed in steroidogenic organs.
source: A sterol homeostatic role has also been suggested for the mouse GramD1b (Aster-B) protein, which is highly expressed in steroidogenic organs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Adrenal glands from a GramD1b knockout mouse are devoid of lipid droplets.
source: Thus, adrenal glands from a GramD1b knockout mouse are devoid of lipid droplets and show a severe reduction in cholesteryl ester content (Sandhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Adrenal glands from a GramD1b knockout mouse show a severe reduction in cholesteryl ester content.
source: Thus, adrenal glands from a GramD1b knockout mouse are devoid of lipid droplets and show a severe reduction in cholesteryl ester content (Sandhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Crystal structures of Lam4S2 in apo- and sterol-bound states have been reported.
source: We recently reported crystal structures of the second StARkin domain of Lam4 (here termed Lam4S2) in apo- and sterol-bound states (Jentsch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Lam4S2 has an overall α/β helix-grip fold that forms a capacious binding pocket.
source: The protein has an overall α/β helix-grip fold that forms a capacious binding pocket into which the sterol appears to be admitted head-first, through an aperture at one end, such that its 3-β-hydroxyl head-group is stabilized by direct or water-mediated interactions with polar residues (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: Sterol appears to be admitted head-first into the Lam4S2 binding pocket through an aperture at one end.
source: The protein has an overall α/β helix-grip fold that forms a capacious binding pocket into which the sterol appears to be admitted head-first, through an aperture at one end, such that its 3-β-hydroxyl head-group is stabilized by direct or water-mediated interactions with polar residues (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: The 3-β-hydroxyl head-group of sterol in Lam4S2 is stabilized by direct or water-mediated interactions with polar residues.
source: The protein has an overall α/β helix-grip fold that forms a capacious binding pocket into which the sterol appears to be admitted head-first, through an aperture at one end, such that its 3-β-hydroxyl head-group is stabilized by direct or water-mediated interactions with polar residues (Figure 1A; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: The interior surface of the Lam4S2 binding pocket is surprisingly polar.
source: The interior surface of the binding pocket is surprisingly polar (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) considering the hydrophobicity of its sterol clients, which include cholesterol, ergosterol, dehydroergosterol (DHE) and 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC) (Results [also see Gatta et al., 2015; Jentsch et al., 2018; Gatta et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: Lam4S2 sterol clients include cholesterol, ergosterol, dehydroergosterol (DHE) and 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC).
source: The interior surface of the binding pocket is surprisingly polar (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) considering the hydrophobicity of its sterol clients, which include cholesterol, ergosterol, dehydroergosterol (DHE) and 25-hydroxycholesterol (25HC) (Results [also see Gatta et al., 2015; Jentsch et al., 2018; Gatta et al., 2018]).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations and experimental data.

claim: The surface of Lam4S2 near the entrance to the pocket is decorated with lysine residues.
source: The surface of the protein near the entrance to the pocket is decorated with lysine residues, accounting for the enhanced ability of Lam4S2 to transfer sterol between anionic vesicles compared with its ability to transfer sterol between neutral vesicles (Jentsch et al., 2018); the entryway itself is partially occluded by a flexible loop, termed Ω1 (Figure 1A), whose functional importance in the StARkin family has been well-documented through mutagenesis studies (Horenkamp et al., 2018; Gatta et al., 2018; Iaea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data and citations.

claim: Lysine residues near the entrance to the Lam4S2 pocket account for enhanced sterol transfer between anionic vesicles compared to neutral vesicles.
source: The surface of the protein near the entrance to the pocket is decorated with lysine residues, accounting for the enhanced ability of Lam4S2 to transfer sterol between anionic vesicles compared with its ability to transfer sterol between neutral vesicles (Jentsch et al., 2018); the entryway itself is partially occluded by a flexible loop, termed Ω1 (Figure 1A), whose functional importance in the StARkin family has been well-documented through mutagenesis studies (Horenkamp et al., 2018; Gatta et al., 2018; Iaea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The entryway to the Lam4S2 binding pocket is partially occluded by a flexible loop termed Ω1.
source: The surface of the protein near the entrance to the pocket is decorated with lysine residues, accounting for the enhanced ability of Lam4S2 to transfer sterol between anionic vesicles compared with its ability to transfer sterol between neutral vesicles (Jentsch et al., 2018); the entryway itself is partially occluded by a flexible loop, termed Ω1 (Figure 1A), whose functional importance in the StARkin family has been well-documented through mutagenesis studies (Horenkamp et al., 2018; Gatta et al., 2018; Iaea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data and citations.

claim: The functional importance of the Ω1 loop in the StARkin family has been well-documented through mutagenesis studies.
source: The surface of the protein near the entrance to the pocket is decorated with lysine residues, accounting for the enhanced ability of Lam4S2 to transfer sterol between anionic vesicles compared with its ability to transfer sterol between neutral vesicles (Jentsch et al., 2018); the entryway itself is partially occluded by a flexible loop, termed Ω1 (Figure 1A), whose functional importance in the StARkin family has been well-documented through mutagenesis studies (Horenkamp et al., 2018; Gatta et al., 2018; Iaea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The structures of other Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains are similar to Lam4S2.
source: The structures of other Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains are similar (Sandhu et al., 2018; Horenkamp et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2018), broadly resembling structures of other members of the StARkin superfamily except for one striking feature.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: The wall of the sterol binding cavity in all Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains is fractured along part of its length.
source: The wall of the sterol binding cavity in all Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains is fractured along part of its length, not unlike one of Lucio Fontana's slashed canvases (Candela, 2019), exposing the sterol backbone to bulk solvent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: The fracture in the wall of the sterol binding cavity exposes the sterol backbone to bulk solvent.
source: The wall of the sterol binding cavity in all Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains is fractured along part of its length, not unlike one of Lucio Fontana's slashed canvases (Candela, 2019), exposing the sterol backbone to bulk solvent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by structural data shown in figures.

claim: Lam4S2 docks onto anionic phospholipid membranes via two modes.
source: Our MD simulations reveal that Lam4S2 docks onto anionic phospholipid membranes mainly via two modes, one of which (termed Mode 2 here) is likely to be physiologically relevant.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Mode 2 of Lam4S2 membrane binding is likely to be physiologically relevant.
source: Our MD simulations reveal that Lam4S2 docks onto anionic phospholipid membranes mainly via two modes, one of which (termed Mode 2 here) is likely to be physiologically relevant.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data and functional tests.

claim: In Mode 2, Lam4S2 engages the membrane via its Ω1 loop and C-terminal helix.
source: In this mode, the protein engages the membrane via its Ω1 loop and C-terminal helix, two structural regions that have been identified previously as being functionally important in StART domains (Jentsch et al., 2018; Horenkamp et al., 2018; Gatta et al., 2018; Iaea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: The Ω1 loop and C-terminal helix have been identified previously as functionally important in StART domains.
source: In this mode, the protein engages the membrane via its Ω1 loop and C-terminal helix, two structural regions that have been identified previously as being functionally important in StART domains (Jentsch et al., 2018; Horenkamp et al., 2018; Gatta et al., 2018; Iaea et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: The side-opening in sterol-loaded Lam4S2 can be occluded by the polar side-chains of residues S181, D61, and K89.
source: The side-opening in sterol-loaded Lam4S2 can be occluded by the polar side-chains of residues S181, D61, and K89, resulting in a low level of hydration within the cavity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Occlusion of the side-opening by S181, D61, and K89 results in a low level of hydration within the cavity.
source: The side-opening in sterol-loaded Lam4S2 can be occluded by the polar side-chains of residues S181, D61, and K89, resulting in a low level of hydration within the cavity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: When the side-opening is occluded, the cholesterol molecule is stably bound with its hydroxyl group forming hydrogen-bonding interactions with residue Q121.
source: In this condition, the cholesterol molecule is stably bound, with its hydroxyl group forming hydrogen-bonding interactions with residue Q121.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Cholesterol egress is triggered stochastically by gradual widening of the side-opening and concomitant penetration of water into the binding site.
source: Cholesterol egress is triggered stochastically, by gradual widening of the side-opening and concomitant penetration of water into the binding site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Widening of the side-opening and water penetration destabilize cholesterol in the binding site by ~4–5 kcal/mole.
source: These dynamic events destabilize cholesterol in the binding site by ~4–5 kcal/mole, driving it from the binding site towards the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by PMF calculations from MD simulations.

claim: Subsequent steps of cholesterol release are enabled by repositioning of the Ω1 loop away from the C-terminal helix.
source: The subsequent steps of the release process are enabled by repositioning of the Ω1 loop away from the C-terminal helix.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Repositioning of the Ω1 loop fully exposes the binding pocket to the membrane, creating a continuous passageway.
source: This fully exposes the binding pocket to the membrane, that is widens the axial aperture, thus creating a continuous passageway to the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: The overall process of cholesterol release from Lam4S2 requires overcoming an energy barrier of ~6 kcal/mole.
source: The overall process of cholesterol release requires that an energy barrier of ~6 kcal/mole is overcome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by PMF calculations from MD simulations.

claim: The energy barrier for cholesterol release from Lam4S2 (~6 kcal/mole) is in reasonable agreement with estimates based on transport rate measurements (~10–15 kcal/mole).
source: This value is in reasonable agreement with the ~10–15 kcal/mole estimate for the energy barrier for sterol extraction by Lam4S2 based on (i) measurement of its transport rate, (ii) the assumption that intermembrane sterol transfer is rate-limited by sterol pick-up/delivery, and (iii) the observation that the rate constant for this process can be described by a simple Arrhenius relationship (Dittman and Menon, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by comparison of computational and experimental data.

claim: The K89A mutation lowers the energy barrier for cholesterol release by ~2 fold compared to wild type Lam4S2.
source: Using potential of mean force calculations, we found that the K89A mutation lowered the energy barrier for cholesterol release by ~2 fold compared with that for wild type Lam4S2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by PMF calculations from MD simulations.

claim: The K89A mutant of Lam4S2 is non-functional.
source: Experimental tests confirmed that the K89A mutant was non-functional, whereas the S181A mutant was only partially compromised in its ability to bind sterol, a defect that did not appear to influence its ability to rescue the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ cells or to exchange sterols between membranes in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: The S181A mutant of Lam4S2 is only partially compromised in its ability to bind sterol.
source: Experimental tests confirmed that the K89A mutant was non-functional, whereas the S181A mutant was only partially compromised in its ability to bind sterol, a defect that did not appear to influence its ability to rescue the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ cells or to exchange sterols between membranes in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: The sterol-binding defect of the S181A mutant does not influence its ability to rescue the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
source: Experimental tests confirmed that the K89A mutant was non-functional, whereas the S181A mutant was only partially compromised in its ability to bind sterol, a defect that did not appear to influence its ability to rescue the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ cells or to exchange sterols between membranes in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: The sterol-binding defect of the S181A mutant does not influence its ability to exchange sterols between membranes in vitro.
source: Experimental tests confirmed that the K89A mutant was non-functional, whereas the S181A mutant was only partially compromised in its ability to bind sterol, a defect that did not appear to influence its ability to rescue the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ cells or to exchange sterols between membranes in vitro.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: The D61A mutant performs as well as wild-type protein in rescuing the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
source: Our test of the D61A mutant was limited to a cell-based assay in which it performed as well as the wild-type protein in rescuing the nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data.

claim: K89 and S181 are among the residues with the highest conservation score in the Lam/GramD1 family.
source: Considering the functional importance of K89, and to a lesser extent S181, we examined the conservation of these residues in the Lam/GramD1 family using a previously reported structure-based sequence alignment (Horenkamp et al., 2018). We found that the positions aligning with K89 and S181 were among the residues with the highest conservation score.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Residue K910 in Lam2S1 aligns with K89 of Lam4S2.
source: Interestingly, it has been noted that the side-chain of residue K910 in the S1 domain of Lam2 (Lam2S1), which aligns with K89 of Lam4S2 (note that K89 in Lam4S2 corresponds to K1031 in the full-length protein [Table 1]) is positioned slightly differently in the ergosterol-bound and apo structures (Horenkamp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by structural comparison and citations.

claim: The side-chain of residue K910 in Lam2S1 is positioned slightly differently in the ergosterol-bound and apo structures.
source: Interestingly, it has been noted that the side-chain of residue K910 in the S1 domain of Lam2 (Lam2S1), which aligns with K89 of Lam4S2 (note that K89 in Lam4S2 corresponds to K1031 in the full-length protein [Table 1]) is positioned slightly differently in the ergosterol-bound and apo structures (Horenkamp et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Movement of K910 in Lam2S1 could enable a path for ergosterol movement into and out of the protein.
source: This led to speculation that a path for ergosterol movement into and out of Lam2S1 could be enabled by movement of K910.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations.

claim: Residue K89 in Lam4S2 repositions when cholesterol is released from the protein.
source: Consistent with this, our study reveals that residue K89 in Lam4S2 does indeed reposition when cholesterol is released from the protein.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Movement of K89 is part of larger-scale dynamic changes involving neighboring polar residues D61 and S181 that lead to widening of the side-opening.
source: Importantly, we find that this movement is a part of larger-scale dynamic changes involving neighboring polar residues, D61 and S181, that lead to widening of the side-opening to the binding pocket.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Lam4S2 associates with membranes via its Ω1 loop and C-terminal helix in Mode 2.
source: In one mode (Mode 1, occurring with ~85% frequency [Figure 1C]), the protein interacted with lipid headgroups via its N- and C-termini (green and red; Figure 1D). In the second mode (Mode 2), observed with ~15% frequency, Lam4S2 engaged with the membrane via its Ω1 loop (purple; Figure 1C,E) and its C-terminal helix (yellow; Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: Mode 1 of Lam4S2 membrane binding occurs with ~85% frequency in simulations.
source: In one mode (Mode 1, occurring with ~85% frequency [Figure 1C]), the protein interacted with lipid headgroups via its N- and C-termini (green and red; Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: Mode 2 of Lam4S2 membrane binding occurs with ~15% frequency in simulations.
source: In the second mode (Mode 2), observed with ~15% frequency, Lam4S2 engaged with the membrane via its Ω1 loop (purple; Figure 1C,E) and its C-terminal helix (yellow; Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: Both modes of Lam4S2 membrane binding are driven by electrostatic interactions between the protein and the membrane surface.
source: Consistent with the overall electrostatic properties of the protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), both modes of binding are driven by electrostatic interactions between the protein and the membrane surface.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data and electrostatic calculations shown in figures.

claim: Mode 1 is stabilized by contacts between the membrane and the basic C-terminus region (e.g. K203), K62, and the positively charged N-terminal amino group.
source: Thus, Mode 1 implicates the protein face composed of the basic C-terminus region (e.g. K203) and nearby K62 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) as well as the positively charged N-terminal amino group, whereas Mode 2 is stabilized by contacts between the membrane and basic residues K163/K167 on the C-terminal helix and K98 in the Ω1 loop region.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: Mode 2 is stabilized by contacts between the membrane and basic residues K163/K167 on the C-terminal helix and K98 in the Ω1 loop region.
source: Thus, Mode 1 implicates the protein face composed of the basic C-terminus region (e.g. K203) and nearby K62 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) as well as the positively charged N-terminal amino group, whereas Mode 2 is stabilized by contacts between the membrane and basic residues K163/K167 on the C-terminal helix and K98 in the Ω1 loop region.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Mode 1 is probably a non-physiological consequence of simulating the isolated Lam4S2 domain.
source: Although more frequent, Mode 1 is probably a non-physiological consequence of simulating the isolated Lam4S2 domain.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by reasoning about the construct used in simulations.

claim: In Mode 1, the hydrophobic tail of cholesterol is directly exposed to the solvent.
source: Furthermore, in this mode, Lam4S2 is positioned on the membrane in such a way that the hydrophobic tail of cholesterol is directly exposed to the solvent (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by structural snapshots from MD simulations shown in figures.

claim: In Mode 2, cholesterol is oriented orthogonally to the plane of membrane with its 3-β-OH group engaging Q121 and its iso-octyl tail facing the membrane.
source: Moreover, in Mode 2, cholesterol is oriented orthogonally to the plane of membrane, with its 3-β-OH group engaging Q121 in the binding pocket of Lam4S2 and its iso-octyl tail facing the membrane (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by structural snapshots from MD simulations shown in figures.

claim: The K163D/K167D double mutant of Lam4S2 binds to membrane vesicles indistinguishably from the wild type protein.
source: The double mutant binds to membrane vesicles indistinguishably from the wild type protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), but fails to transport sterol between vesicles, as we previously reported (Jentsch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations.

claim: The K163D/K167D double mutant of Lam4S2 fails to transport sterol between vesicles.
source: The double mutant binds to membrane vesicles indistinguishably from the wild type protein (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), but fails to transport sterol between vesicles, as we previously reported (Jentsch et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: The K163D/K167D mutations destabilize Mode 2 and drive Lam4S2 to exclusively adopt the Mode 1 pose on the membrane surface.
source: These results suggest that this mutant, like the wild-type protein, binds the membrane predominantly via the unproductive Mode 1 form of association, which is unperturbed by the mutations. However, unlike the wild-type protein, the double mutant is unable to populate Mode 2. Indeed, when the K163D/K167D mutation was introduced into the computational model of Lam4S2 representing binding Mode 2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), and the resulting system was subjected to ~50 ns MD simulations, we observed a spontaneous reorientation of the protein-membrane complex to the Mode 1 pose (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E). These results suggest that the K163D/K167D mutations destabilize Mode 2 and drive Lam4S2 to exclusively adopt the Mode 1 pose on the membrane surface.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: Mode 1 is functionally irrelevant for Lam4S2 sterol transport activity.
source: Importantly, given that the double mutant is functionally inactive, these observations confirm that Mode 1 is functionally irrelevant.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental and computational data.

claim: Widening of the side-entrance to the sterol-binding site is enabled by gradual separation of the side-chains of residues D61 and S181.
source: The first step in the sterol-release process involves widening of the side-entrance to the sterol-binding site, which is enabled by gradual separation of the side-chains of residues D61 and S181.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Concomitant with the widening of the side-opening, the level of hydration of the binding pocket progressively increases.
source: Concomitant with the widening of the side-opening, the level of hydration (water count) of the binding pocket progressively increases (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: Cholesterol remains stably bound during the initial widening of the side-opening and increase in hydration.
source: Cholesterol remains stably bound throughout these initial events (cholesterol RMSD is unchanged in Microstates 1–3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: Rising hydration in the binding site results in destabilization of polar interactions between the 3-β-OH of cholesterol and the side-chain of Q121.
source: However, the rising level of hydration in the binding site results in destabilization of the polar interactions between the 3-β-OH group of cholesterol and the side-chain of residue Q121 as cholesterol initiates its translocation towards the membrane.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: The sterol translocation process was sampled in its entirety in 5 out of 100 Stage 2 simulations.
source: The sterol translocation process outlined above was sampled in its entirety in 5 out of 100 Stage 2 simulations (trajectories highlighted in red in Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: 19 trajectories in Stage 2 simulations sampled the evolution of the system from Microstate 1 to Microstate 5.
source: Another 19 trajectories in this set sampled the evolution of the system from Microstate 1 to Microstate 5 (trajectories marked with a green star in Figure 2—figure supplement 4), but on the time scales of these simulations, the system either did not progress further (i.e. to Microstates 6 and 7) or returned to Microstate 4 or 3 where it remained (see also below).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: D61 is engaged in electrostatic interactions with residue K89 located in the β2 strand preceding the Ω1 loop.
source: We found that D61 is engaged in electrostatic interactions with residue K89 located in the β2 strand preceding the Ω1 loop.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: The side-chain of K89 faces the entrance of the binding pocket where it interacts with the anionic side-chain of D61.
source: Thus, the side-chain of K89 faces the entrance of the binding pocket where it interacts with the anionic side-chain of D61 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: The D61-K89 interaction is maintained in the initial stages of the translocation process (Microstates 1–4).
source: This interaction is maintained in the initial stages of the translocation process (Microstates 1–4), but becomes unstable as the hydration of the sterol-binding pocket reaches its highest levels after cholesterol leaves the site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; also note sampling of a wide range of d61–89 distances for Microstates 5–7 in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: The D61-K89 interaction becomes unstable as the hydration of the sterol-binding pocket reaches its highest levels after cholesterol leaves the site.
source: This interaction is maintained in the initial stages of the translocation process (Microstates 1–4), but becomes unstable as the hydration of the sterol-binding pocket reaches its highest levels after cholesterol leaves the site (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; also note sampling of a wide range of d61–89 distances for Microstates 5–7 in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: D61, S181 and K89 together participate in stabilizing the closed conformation of the side-entrance to the binding pocket.
source: These data suggest that D61, S181 and K89 together participate in stabilizing the closed conformation of the side-entrance to the binding pocket.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data.

claim: For all three mutations (K89A, D61A and S181A), the hydration level of the sterol-binding site increased rapidly during the initial 4–5 ns of the simulations.
source: Analysis of these trajectories revealed that for all three of the mutants, the hydration level of the sterol-binding site increased rapidly during the initial 4–5 ns of the simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: In the trajectories for the mutant proteins (K89A, D61A, S181A), cholesterol was destabilized in its binding pocket.
source: Furthermore, in the trajectories for the mutant proteins, cholesterol was destabilized in its binding pocket (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: For the K89A system, in all but one replicate, the sterol was unstable in its binding site.
source: On the simulation timescales, rapid destabilization was especially notable for the K89A system in which, for all but one replicate, the sterol was unstable in its binding site (panel labeled K89A, Figure 2—figure supplement 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: For the wild-type Lam4S2 system, cholesterol release requires that an energy barrier of ~6 kcal/mole is overcome.
source: For the wild-type system, the PMF calculations indicate that cholesterol release requires that an energy barrier of ~6 kcal/mole is overcome, and proceeds through two major steps that were also identified in our tICA analysis of Stage 2 simulations.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PMF calculations from umbrella sampling MD simulations.

claim: Cholesterol release from wild-type Lam4S2 proceeds through two major steps identified in tICA analysis.
source: For the wild-type system, the PMF calculations indicate that cholesterol release requires that an energy barrier of ~6 kcal/mole is overcome, and proceeds through two major steps that were also identified in our tICA analysis of Stage 2 simulations.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PMF calculations and tICA analysis from MD simulations.

claim: The K89A mutation significantly lowers the barriers that must be overcome for transition between different energy minima during cholesterol release.
source: Remarkably, comparison of the PMF plots for the wild-type and the K89A systems (Figure 4A) reveals that the mutation significantly lowers the barriers that must be overcome in order for transition between the different energy minima to occur.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PMF calculations shown in figures.

claim: The energy barrier for the entire cholesterol release process in K89A Lam4S2 is ~3 kcal/mole.
source: Thus, although the PMF profile for the K89A construct still has three energy minima, the energy cost of transitioning between the global minimum and LM-1 in this system is ~2 kcal/mole, and between LM-2 and LM-3 is ~1 kcal/mole, resulting in an energy barrier of only ~3 kcal/mole for the entire release process (dZ(chol–121)∈ [2 Å; 20 Å]).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PMF calculations from umbrella sampling MD simulations.

claim: The energy barrier for cholesterol release in K89A Lam4S2 is approximately half of that determined for the wild-type system.
source: This is approximately half of that determined for the wild-type system.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by PMF calculations from umbrella sampling MD simulations.

claim: The reduction in energy cost for cholesterol release in K89A can be explained by the greater extent of hydration of the binding site compared to wild-type protein.
source: This reduction in the energy cost can be explained by the greater extent of hydration of the binding site in K89A compared to that in the wild-type protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by analysis of MD simulation data.

claim: In wild-type Lam4S2, the binding site remains largely dehydrated until cholesterol disengages from Q121.
source: Indeed, in wild-type Lam4S2, the binding site remains largely dehydrated until cholesterol disengages from Q121 (dZ(chol–121)∈ [2 Å; 6 Å]) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), whereas in the K89A protein, the level of solvation of the binding pocket is relatively high (>10 water molecules) even when cholesterol is interacting with Q121 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: In the K89A protein, the level of solvation of the binding pocket is relatively high (>10 water molecules) even when cholesterol is interacting with Q121.
source: Indeed, in wild-type Lam4S2, the binding site remains largely dehydrated until cholesterol disengages from Q121 (dZ(chol–121)∈ [2 Å; 6 Å]) (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), whereas in the K89A protein, the level of solvation of the binding pocket is relatively high (>10 water molecules) even when cholesterol is interacting with Q121 (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by MD simulation data shown in figures.

claim: Yeast cells lacking Ysp2/Lam2 (lam2Δ cells) are sensitive to the polyene antibiotic amphotericin B.
source: We previously showed that yeast cells lacking Ysp2/Lam2 (lam2Δ cells) are sensitive to the polyene antibiotic amphotericin B, and that this phenotype can be corrected by expression of a soluble GFP–Lam4S2 fusion protein (Gatta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: The amphotericin B sensitivity phenotype of lam2Δ cells can be corrected by expression of a soluble GFP–Lam4S2 fusion protein.
source: We previously showed that yeast cells lacking Ysp2/Lam2 (lam2Δ cells) are sensitive to the polyene antibiotic amphotericin B, and that this phenotype can be corrected by expression of a soluble GFP–Lam4S2 fusion protein (Gatta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citations.

claim: lam2Δ cells are sensitive to nystatin.
source: We verified that this was also the case for nystatin, another polyene antibiotic (Figure 5A, compare the first two rows in which lam2Δ cells are transformed with either an empty vector (row 1) or a vector for expression of GFP–Lam4S2 (row 2, WT), and plated on media without nystatin or with different amounts of nystatin).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Expression of GFP–Lam4S2 corrects the nystatin sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
source: We verified that this was also the case for nystatin, another polyene antibiotic (Figure 5A, compare the first two rows in which lam2Δ cells are transformed with either an empty vector (row 1) or a vector for expression of GFP–Lam4S2 (row 2, WT), and plated on media without nystatin or with different amounts of nystatin).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: lam2Δ cells expressing GFP–Lam4S2(K89A) remained nystatin-sensitive.
source: Figure 5A shows that lam2Δ cells expressing GFP–Lam4S2(K89A) remained nystatin-sensitive, whereas those expressing GFP–Lam4S2(D61A) or GFP–Lam4S2(S181A) became resistant to the antibiotic, similar to lam2Δ cells expressing wild-type protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: lam2Δ cells expressing GFP–Lam4S2(D61A) or GFP–Lam4S2(S181A) became resistant to nystatin, similar to lam2Δ cells expressing wild-type protein.
source: Figure 5A shows that lam2Δ cells expressing GFP–Lam4S2(K89A) remained nystatin-sensitive, whereas those expressing GFP–Lam4S2(D61A) or GFP–Lam4S2(S181A) became resistant to the antibiotic, similar to lam2Δ cells expressing wild-type protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: All Lam4S2 variants tested (WT, K89A, D61A, S181A) were expressed at equivalent levels.
source: As all the Lam4S2 variants tested were expressed at equivalent levels (as revealed by SDS-PAGE immunoblotting [Figure 5B]), this cell-based assay indicates that the K89A mutant has a functional deficit, whereas the D61A and S181A proteins are able to provide cells with sufficient functionality to rescue their nystatin-sensitivity phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The K89A mutant has a functional deficit in rescuing nystatin-sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
source: As all the Lam4S2 variants tested were expressed at equivalent levels (as revealed by SDS-PAGE immunoblotting [Figure 5B]), this cell-based assay indicates that the K89A mutant has a functional deficit, whereas the D61A and S181A proteins are able to provide cells with sufficient functionality to rescue their nystatin-sensitivity phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data.

claim: The D61A and S181A proteins are able to provide cells with sufficient functionality to rescue their nystatin-sensitivity phenotype.
source: As all the Lam4S2 variants tested were expressed at equivalent levels (as revealed by SDS-PAGE immunoblotting [Figure 5B]), this cell-based assay indicates that the K89A mutant has a functional deficit, whereas the D61A and S181A proteins are able to provide cells with sufficient functionality to rescue their nystatin-sensitivity phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data.

claim: The S181A mutant extracted only ~50% of sterol compared to wild-type protein under standard incubation conditions.
source: Relative to the wild-type protein, the S181A mutant extracted only ~50% of sterol under our standard incubation conditions, whereas the K89A mutant had essentially no ability to extract sterol (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The K89A mutant had essentially no ability to extract sterol from membranes.
source: Relative to the wild-type protein, the S181A mutant extracted only ~50% of sterol under our standard incubation conditions, whereas the K89A mutant had essentially no ability to extract sterol (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Under standard conditions, wild-type Lam4S2 increases the rate of DHE exchange ~7 fold over the spontaneous rate.
source: Figure 7B (see also Figure 7D) shows that under our standard conditions, the wild-type protein increases the rate of DHE exchange ~7 fold over the spontaneous rate.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The performance of the S181A mutant in sterol exchange assays was similar to that of the wild-type protein.
source: The performance of the S181A mutant was similar to that of the wild-type protein, whereas the K89A mutant had essentially no activity (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The K89A mutant had essentially no sterol exchange activity.
source: The performance of the S181A mutant was similar to that of the wild-type protein, whereas the K89A mutant had essentially no activity (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The K89A mutant is unable to extract sterol from membranes or to transfer it between vesicles.
source: Overall, the three functional tests described above indicate that the K89A mutant is compromised in sterol handling—it is unable to extract sterol from membranes or to transfer it between vesicles, accounting for its inability to rescue the nystatin sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data.

claim: The inability of K89A to extract or transfer sterol accounts for its inability to rescue the nystatin sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
source: Overall, the three functional tests described above indicate that the K89A mutant is compromised in sterol handling—it is unable to extract sterol from membranes or to transfer it between vesicles, accounting for its inability to rescue the nystatin sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data.

claim: The functional outcomes for K89A are in line with the computational prediction that cholesterol would be unstable in the binding site of Lam4S2 K89A.
source: These functional outcomes are in line with our computational prediction that cholesterol would be unstable in the binding site of the Lam4S2 K89A.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by comparison of computational and experimental data.

claim: The partial inability of the S181A mutant to extract cholesterol did not affect its ability to catalyze sterol exchange.
source: Interestingly, the partial inability of the S181A mutant to extract cholesterol did not affect its ability to catalyze sterol exchange or to rescue the nystatin sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data.

claim: The partial inability of the S181A mutant to extract cholesterol did not affect its ability to rescue the nystatin sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
source: Interestingly, the partial inability of the S181A mutant to extract cholesterol did not affect its ability to catalyze sterol exchange or to rescue the nystatin sensitivity of lam2Δ cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by experimental data.

claim: Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains specifically bind sterols.
source: Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains specifically bind sterols (Gatta et al., 2015), admitting and exporting the sterol molecule through an aperture at the end of their long axis as suggested by inspection of crystal structures (Sandhu et al., 2018; Jentsch et al., 2018; Horenkamp et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2018) and as also seen in the MD simulations reported here.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations and MD simulation data.

claim: Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains admit and export sterol through an aperture at the end of their long axis.
source: Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains specifically bind sterols (Gatta et al., 2015), admitting and exporting the sterol molecule through an aperture at the end of their long axis as suggested by inspection of crystal structures (Sandhu et al., 2018; Jentsch et al., 2018; Horenkamp et al., 2018; Tong et al., 2018) and as also seen in the MD simulations reported here.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citations and MD simulation data.

claim: Sterol egress (or entry) from Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains is controlled by the concomitant entry (or egress) of water molecules via the lateral fracture.
source: The analyses presented here describe a potentially general mechanism by which sterol egress (or entry) from Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains is controlled by the concomitant entry (or egress) of water molecules via this unusual lateral fracture.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data and experimental validation.

claim: The mechanism of sterol egress controlled by water entry via the lateral fracture is potentially general for Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains.
source: The analyses presented here describe a potentially general mechanism by which sterol egress (or entry) from Lam/GramD1 StARkin domains is controlled by the concomitant entry (or egress) of water molecules via this unusual lateral fracture.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by MD simulation data and structural comparisons.
